wsl-claude: only drop half of them, please. The two groups differ:
- The node's OWN EVENTS (claim, claim-refused, partner-added, invite-minted...) must STAY. They ARE your owner notices: the log hands them out through ownerEvents() (trafficLog.js:468, tested in ownerLog.js). Dropping them breaks this plan's first rule, 'nothing above trafficLog.js changes'.
- The REFUSED-BEFORE-SEALING rows can go if you like: nothing reads them for a feature. But they're the only record that a post was attempted and failed; that's how the 11,628 unsent reports were found. They're small. I'd keep new ones and let old ones age out, but it's your call.
And a bonus the move brings: trafficLog.js:225-240 documents a real bug in ownerEvents. It asks 'everything since this TIME', two events in the same millisecond, and the second, often the claim-refused you wanted, is silently lost. With the sequence number, readers ask 'everything since row N' instead, and nothing can be skipped.

at some point wouldn't they get flushed/shedded by design?

No, by your own decision. trafficLog.js:71-73: 'PERMANENT. Andy: the log should be permanent. period.' And :536-537: 'nothing is pruned at all'. README/CAPACITY.md says the same: the log is your side of every exchange, so it's the one file to watch on a small disk. So nothing gets shed today. If you want refused attempts, or anything else, to age out, that's a new retention rule and a reversal of 'permanent. period.', so it would be its own item here. The database makes it cheap: one DELETE by kind and age. Do you want it?

wsl-claude: not today, by your own ruling: trafficLog.js:71-73, 'Andy: "the log should be permanent. period."' It once had a 24-hour window, which was removed, and the file says 'nothing in this file ages out, whether it was read, refused, ignored or sent' and 'THIS FILE GROWS WITHOUT BOUND. That is the decision, not a bug.' So shedding would be a new decision, reversing that one, and it's yours to make.
It also sharpens the risk I raised: node.db has a 20 MB size cap that EVICTS to stay under it. A log that is permanent by decision, living in that same file, will eventually meet that cap, and the eviction would throw away what the node knows about peers, never the log. So with 'permanent', the log can't count against node.db's cap: either its own file, or the cap measured without it.

one key by hash should be there anyways, so that the pair of record carrying the same has can be found quickly?
one key by hash should be there anyways, so that the pair of record carrying the same has can be found quickly?

Yes, that's the index on hash we already have in the shape: not unique, just fast. Finding a request and its reply becomes one lookup instead of reading the whole file. Rows with a blank hash simply aren't found by it, which is right, because they have no pair.
